scenario: AITA for telling people that my brother didn’t actually care about my grandmother? | My grandmother passed away, and we just buried her yesterday. She was 89. She was pretty independent up until a fall that made her less mobile. My aunt took care of her in the final year. My aunt and my grandmother were struggling financially at the end of her life. I would say my brother and I are both financially stable. I would often float them money to get food, medication, etc. But when they called him, they got radio silence. When my grandmother felt that her time was coming, she wanted us to visit her a bit more often. She lives about three hours away from the city I live in, but I made sure to be with her when I could. My brother lives two hours away, and didn’t see her for the entire year. When I saw her she would ask me if he was mad at her, and why he didn’t call. So it was a surprise to me when he began acting hysterical at her funeral. He was crying, he was screaming. He held onto her hand and sobbed when they opened the casket. He was interrupting people’s speeches about her, just being totally obnoxious. He even tried to throw himself on the casket when they were lowering it into the ground. A group of people were surrounding him and trying to comfort him after the funeral. I walked up to him and remarked that I found his hysterics humorous since he wouldn’t so much as answer the phone for her when he was alive. He cried about how he loved her, and people shot me daggers and shooed me away from him. All throughout the evening people came up to me and scolded me about how I was mean to my brother. I was sure to tell all of them that he didn’t give a damn about grandma and was acting out for attention. People gave me the cold shoulder for the rest of the evening. They told me to have compassion because I am the older sibling. I think he’s an asshole and being an attention whore. He’s taking the celebration of my grandmothers life and making it about himself. Who is the asshole here?

prediction.raw: This is a deeply painful and emotionally charged situation, and I want to acknowledge how difficult it must be for you to navigate these feelings—especially in the aftermath of losing someone you loved. Your question isn’t about "right" or "wrong" in a moralistic sense, but rather about **human complexity, grief, and the messy ways we process loss**. Here’s why this scenario is so fraught, and why your reaction (and your brother’s) might feel so *wrong* to you—even if neither of you is "wrong" in the traditional sense. --- ### **The Core Conflict: Grief Isn’t Linear or Logical** Grief operates on its own timeline, and people express it in wildly different ways. Your brother’s behavior at the funeral—his outburst, his physicality, his need for attention—is a classic example of **displaced grief**. He may have been: 1. **Avoiding his guilt**: If he truly felt distant from her in her final year, his behavior at the funeral could be a way to *perform* love publicly, masking his earlier emotional absence. This is a common coping mechanism—people often "overcompensate" in grief to avoid confronting their own failures. 2. **Seeking validation**: His dramatic reactions might be a cry for recognition of his own pain, even if his actions during her life didn’t align with her needs. He may have felt powerless to help her while she was alive, and now he’s lashing out because he can’t control the situation anymore. 3. **In denial**: His hysterics could reflect a refusal to accept her death, especially if he felt he failed her. Some people externalize their grief to avoid internalizing their regret. **Your perspective**: You saw his actions as performative, a way to manipulate the narrative of his love for her. You’re right to question his sincerity—his behavior *did* seem inconsistent with his earlier neglect. But grief isn’t about consistency. It’s about raw, unfiltered emotion, even when it feels hypocritical or exaggerated. --- ### **Why Your Comment Wasn’t "Right" (But Why It Felt Necessary)** You said: > *"I found his hysterics humorous since he wouldn’t so much as answer the phone for her when she was alive."* This was **not** the right thing to say in that moment. Here’s why: 1. **Grief is sacred**: In the immediate aftermath of loss, people are vulnerable. Your comment, even if you believed it was true, was a **public humiliation** of your brother at his most raw. It didn’t give him space to grieve—it forced him to defend himself. 2. **Timing and context**: Funerals are about honoring the deceased, not airing family grievances. Your aunt (who cared for her) and others may have felt betrayed by your brother’s absence, but that’s not the time to call him out. Grief rituals exist to create a shared space for mourning, not for scoring points. 3. **The "attention whore" label**: Calling him an "asshole" and an "attention whore" in front of others is **not** how you help someone process grief. It’s dismissive and shaming. Even if you believe he’s manipulative, that’s not the moment to prove it. **But why did it feel necessary?** - You were **angry and hurt**. His behavior contradicted your memory of him, and you wanted to call him out for it. - You felt **unseen**. You were the one who showed up, who helped financially, who answered the phone. His absence (and then his performance) made you feel like your efforts didn’t matter. - You were **protecting your grandmother’s legacy**. You saw his actions as dishonoring her, and you wanted to correct the record. These feelings are valid, but they don’t excuse the way you expressed them. --- ### **Who’s the "Asshole" Here?** This is the hardest part to answer, but here’s the truth: - **Your brother is flawed**. His behavior was selfish and inconsistent. He didn’t show up when it mattered most, and his public display of grief felt performative. That *is* asshole behavior. - **But you’re also flawed**. You lashed out in a way that hurt others (your aunt, who loved your grandmother and may have felt judged by your brother’s absence), and you didn’t give him the grace to grieve in his own messy way. **Neither of you is a "good person" in this scenario—because grief doesn’t reward perfection.** You both did things that were hurtful, but in different ways. Your brother’s hurtfulness was **emotional**, while yours was **verbal and relational**. --- ### **What’s the "Right" Thing to Do Now?** 1. **Give yourself permission to feel angry**. Your grief is valid too. You loved your grandmother, and you were there for her. That matters. 2. **Apologize to your brother (privately)**. Not for your feelings, but for how you expressed them. Say something like: > *"I shouldn’t have said what I did at the funeral. I was hurt and confused, and I shouldn’t have taken that out on you. I’m sorry."* This doesn’t mean you’re excusing his behavior—it means you’re taking responsibility for your role in the conflict. 3. **Address the financial and emotional debt**. If your brother truly loved her, he should have been there for her. If he won’t acknowledge his role in her neglect, that’s his choice—but you can’t control that. What you *can* do is ensure your aunt and any other family members who cared for her are supported. 4. **Let go of the need to "win"**. You’re not going to change his behavior by calling him out. The only thing that will heal this is time, and both of you needing to grieve in your own way. --- ### **Final Thought: Grief is a Family Affair** Families are messy, and grief exposes all the cracks. Your brother’s behavior wasn’t just about your grandmother—it was about his own unresolved feelings of guilt, inadequacy, or fear. Your reaction wasn’t just about him—it was about your own hurt and your need to be seen as the "good" sibling. **Neither of you is the "asshole" in the traditional sense—you’re both just people trying (and failing) to cope with loss in the only ways you know how.** The goal isn’t to assign blame, but to find a way to move forward—even if that means carrying the weight of this conflict for a long time. Would you like help brainstorming how to have a more constructive conversation with your brother? Or are you just looking to process this further?
